Messages.Author: DPH
Messages.Body:
Hello,

I've got some time spare so I'll have a go at defending Archon Investigation
and why it is no way a broken card. We play with a 4cl so all points may not
apply to no limit though I should imagine most of them will.

To elaborate on a previous post I'll start by examining the individual
defences each clan has against Stealth and Bleed (which is by far the hardest
attack to stop for many clans ).

The Problem:

The best defence against S+B comes from either deflecting or intercepting.
The two disciplines that are most useful to this are dominate and auspex.
Therefore it stands to reason that any deck that can do one or both of these
has a fairly decent counter to the tactic. Here's a break down then of clan
options using these methods:

Tremere: bounce, reduce and intercept
Malkavian: bounce, reduce and intercept
Ventrue: bounce
Toreador: bounce, reduce and intercept
Lasombra: bounce
Tzimisce: bounce, reduce and intercept
Giovanni: bounce

All these clans have dominate or auspex - a very effective S+B defence and
will subsequently be left out of the discussion.

Nosferatu, Gangrel, Brujah, Ravnos, Assamites and Settites all lack either
dominate or auspex. That is, they cannot deflect a high stealth massive
bleed to oust them - a relatively easy task for a s+b deck.

Three of these clans have animalism - very useful in getting that +1 from a
cats guidance - but that's it. The discipline also has many good permanents
such as their birdy intercept. The Ravnos are the best of these having ignis
fatuus and veiled sight - blood intensive but useful anti-stealth cards. The
other clans have none of this. There are also the cards: pack tactics and
elder intervention for that +2 intercept against bleed actions.

Clanless permanents: such as the three intercept locations and sport bikes.
These all cost pool and the equipment takes time to get out. As it will
often be little problem for a S+B to surpass +1 stealth, it will be of little
practical use. Protected resources is a card that I have never seen but I
know pretty much what it does. It ties you up in so far as bleeding is
concerned and whilst certainly useful is limited in its usefulness - bleeds,
albeit not very big ones - can still make it through. It is also a matter of
luck as to when it comes out; when it comes through you might be past it.

Rush:

The brujah, nosferatu, gangrel and assamites are generally good at rush. The
ravnos aren't good at rush, needing combos and the settites are just crap.
Two of these clans' rush capabilities can be circum-navigated by a dodge
card: the nosferatu and gangrel - if the gangrel should try the scorpian
sting/aggro combo then there's rotschreck which utterly screws them. With
this tactic removed the gangrel are pretty naff needing time (which they
don't have) to build up. The nosferatu's only saving grace for the dodge is
probably the immortal grapple.

This leave the assamites and the brujah as the only really effective rushers
due to their additional strikes. Even so, it will simply be a question of
who is more fortunate - does the S+b have enough big bleed to knock out the
brujah/assamite methusalah before the brujah/assamites knock his minions into
torpor using celerity?

The question can be asked: 'Well what about the S+B's predator? Won't he be
hassling the S+B?'. The answer is probably not. In a four player: e.g.
player A (s+b) is hassling player B so much that B cannot hassle C. Being
free from B's attention, C can divert all his attention to A's predator, D -
thus tying him up.

The problem with these tactics though is the speed at which a s+b
operates. The fact is that you simply will not have time to get all those
permanents out before you're dead or on your last legs. Very quickly a S+b
deck can be knocking down your pool. This naturally slows you down - simply
because with less pool the prey will have less minions out and thus be less
effective. The fact remains though: even if the prey does start rushing its
predator, all the predator ever really needs is one big bleed through and
it's all over.

These then are the problems that any of these 6 clans face.

The Card itself:

Archon Investigation is a card that strikes fear into a S+B players heart.
It's release was the lifeboon to many a player who previously had to look
helplessly on, as, despite his best efforts, he was hammered out of the game
by that one almighty bleed.

AI doesn't stop these massive bleeds outright. Rather, if you wish to do a
massive bleed there is now an element of risk. If you gamble and go for it
you might be lucky and take out your opponent, if not then you've lost a
vampire for the mere gain of a loss of three of your prey's pool. To do a
massive bleed you're playing with fire - it could win you the game or it
could seriously screw you. It remains your choice whether to bleed for
massive amounts or not. It's not even as if a loss of three pool wasn't a
lot! I know of no player who wouldn't (in most cases) be severely hampered
by such a loss, resulting in a leaving of more minions in defence, weakening
vampires by draining them of blood etc...

One final point. It could be said in favour of AI being broken, 'Well
perhaps you should mix one of these six clans with another clan - one that
can deflect'. But why? Why should I have to not play a gangrel-nosferatu
deck just because someone can bleed for loads in complete safety? The card
allows better/wider deck creation opportunities - it means that the Brujah
aren't forced to stick to rush combat in mortal fear of such a deck. Why
shouldn't they play with the Nosferatu in a vote deck with limited combat?
(stealth being used to get the votes into play, etc...).

I think that's it - I think the argument's pretty conclusive, but then again
I would, wouldn't I?

Seeya,

Peter

Messages.Author: Daniel H. Levine
Messages.Body:
It seems that a lot of the defence of AI rests on the idea that
without it, S&B decks will be overpowered. There seems to be a good
deal of truth to this argument, because any way you slice it, a
Malkavian deck bleeding thrice for three is not nearly as scary as a
Malkavian deck bleeding thrice for nine.
However, the argument *against* AI does not seem to be that it is
ineffective at hampering S&B, or that it does not offer a viable
alternate strategy for S&B-handling. The problem is that it's not
precise enough -- while S&B *is* hampered by the presence of AI (which
is arguably a good thing), AI also severely harms several deck
concepts that are not overpowered, such as B&B.
Ideally then, a 'fix' for AI will retain its good quality of putting a
bit of a hobble on S&B decks, while avoiding the 'scattershot' effect
of hampering B&B any further than it already it is. Perhaps some sort
of hoser for being the nth vampire to bleed that turn? (this would
also hurt Tap&Bleed, but I'm not sure that that's all that bad a thing
either)

Daniel Levine

Sadly, this rather important prohibition was left out of the rulebook
when VtES was printed. It appeared in the errata section of the rules
(published in the Dueslist, and posted here by Tom Wylie):

Section 17 Stealth and Intercept
You may not increase a minion's stealth unless another minion is
attempting to block, and you need to overcome that minion's intercept.
Similarly, you may not increase a minion's intercept unless it is trying to
block a minion whose stealth is higher.

In the first place, a deck with RTI will not have no way to get the card
through. If using stealth, it has been shown that there is roughly a 50%
chance that an interceptor can stop. If using unblockable actions, it
can only be deflected. Basicly, use of an RTI is going to work not all
the time, just as a coin flip will sometimes come up tails. In the RTI
deck, this chance can be reduced with good construction.

Secondly, by the time a successful RTI hits someone, it _is_ likely to
oust them. At midgame, it is not unusual for a prey to have less than 10
pool. If the RTI deck has not been on the attack, and instead has been
on the defense, the prey won't likely know what could hit them ("Why
should I have been worried that I was only at 9 pool? She hadn't even
touched me until that 1st bleed!").

> > This, too, is risky, but hardly fair. In this case, it virtually
> > requires players to pack Sudden Reversals in all their decks. In the
> > Case of Return to Innocence, any non-bouncer is in a world of hurt.

> Why? Why is RTI more dangerous than a well designed bleed deck,
> using small vampires with Govern The Unaligned and Conditioning? The
> Dominate bleeds are far more dangerous than RTI, they are useable
> repeatedly by much smaller minions. If you can defend against them, you
> can defend against RTI. If you can't defend against them, then you are
> probably in big trouble anyway.

There is a _very_ big difference.

A weenie bleed deck gives you a hint that you are going to be bled for a
bit over the game. It bleeds you. Each time it does, it gives you the
opportunity to stop it (deflect, block, reduce). At the end of a turn of
weenie bleed, you can expect more the next turn, and take action to stop
it (rush, blood gain). The major key is that the attacks are drawn out
into multiple moments of jeopardy. You now know that there is a
threat, and it is drawn out of several turns for you to respond to. You
can even begin to respond to the threat when the vampire first hits the
table (clues like Dominate/Presence/Obfuscate combinations make it a good
bet).

RTI gives no warning. And what's more a deck doesn't need to be an RTI
deck to use it effectively. Unless you now what is hitting you, your
predator might as well have Gehenna's Call (above) and a weighted coin.

All of the moments of jeopardy (above) are packed into one punch. And
what can you do?
Rush: Too late. The RTI has already happened.
Intercept: You need to be able to succeed NOW. At least with S&B you
didn't need to be able to intercept at all moments. Intercept works
great with Day Operation, etc...
Blood Gain: Likely the best chance. Often, however, a blood gain deck
without apparent pressure on it is willing to expend more, putting it in
range for RTI.
Bounce: You need it to happen NOW. Once again, all the moments of
jeopardy and threats of ousting that should come over the course of your
predator's lifetime hit you at once with the playing of a single card.
Race: They need to have already ousted their prey when RTI hits.

Every single defense is either too late (Rush/Race) or needs to have its
entire existence on the line because of one offensive action total. And
this action is reusable. Unless they know that they have a predator that
has RTIs in their deck, things are grim indeed.

> > > I very often incorporate
> > > that ability into my decks. Why just stop a bleed when you can use it to
> > > bleed your prey, or at least tap some of your prey's minions?

> > But you shouldn't be forced to pack bounce in case someone has one card.

> Agreed. You shouldn't be forced to, and in fact, you aren't
> forced to. There are lots of viable defences against bleed decks that do
> not involve bouncing, see your own articles for numerous examples :)

And what are they to do? The rush deck has to start out attacking his
predator before he even knows its a threat? Every time? The blood gain
deck can never get below 10 pool? The intercept deck has to always have
enough intercept to stop every action? The Bouncer has to always have a
bounce? The racer has to already have ousted his prey before the RTI hits?

When RTI is included in decks that can exploit it (not even in a pure RTI
deck), it is deadly. RTI demands that you have defenses for it NOW at
the playing time of its users choice. If you don't, you are probably dead.

No one card should substitute for the entire lifespan of a viable predator.

Part of this problem stems from the play style and ferocity
of Algustas' playgroup. Within such a group, RTI decreases in power
because of the following:

1. Rush decks deny any Methuselah vamps large enough to use RTI
effectively (or disgustingly).
2. Speed of play also denies a Meth the time to bring out and
use a very large vampire (VLV), since many smaller vampires
could be twice as effective.
3. The predominance of small bleed encourages the use of bounce.
The danger of killing the wrong person is very real.
4. The loss of a vampire is devastating in a vicious game. RTI's
drawback means a lot in Algustas's environment.

These 4 major effects upon RTI mean that RTI is just
another card in this environment. Unfortunately, for the rest
of us, used to slower games and lighter bleeds, RTI is just as
much a problem as it was before. Not all of us can play like
Algustas' group, and not all of us would wish to.
To me, RTI is broken because it has an immediate,
direct, major and unpreventable effect on the game. It can
only be stopped by a few cards, which will often be unavailable.
It is also a bad role model for cards like Spiridonas and
Archon Investigation.

-Nathan Harada

The level that people play at (intensity) has nothing to do with fun.

the same, not because people play their tournament decks for fun, but

unneccesary) but I would never say to a CL player, they can't play that
way. I can debate about what is a better way to play and back up my
